history.note: Tracked. Bids closed June 29; no public word yet on how many proposals arrived.

Developer lease proposals closed June 29 and the Air Force is now in private evaluation of bids for up to 12 parcels across JBER, Eielson and Clear. The FY2027 NDAA reported by the Senate Armed Services Committee on June 23 would require a formal grid-impact assessment before the military can approve a data-center Enhanced Use Lease, a statutory check Interior utilities and ratepayers had sought.
Lease proposals were due June 29 and no developer selection or award has been made public as of this run. Carried forward as pending.

A July 19 industry analysis (AIX Energy) notes the Alaska Enhanced Use Lease solicitation for commercial AI data centers on about 4,700 acres across 12 parcels at JBER, Eielson and Clear has moved out of its open proposal phase with no developer award announced, and that unlike the Lower 48 portfolio (which set 100 MW and 500 million dollar minimums) the Alaska request's specific megawatt and capital thresholds are not disclosed. Carried forward as pending decision.

Re-verified by fetching the solicitation record for AFCEC-26-R-0006. Twenty-six days past the deadline the three Alaska installations named in the request, JBER, Eielson Air Force Base and Clear Space Force Station, still have no publicly announced lessee. Evaluation is private, so there is no public comment room here.

Material update from Congress, verified against primary records. On July 22 at 4:37 p.m. the U.S. House passed H.R. 8800, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2027, by 216 yea to 212 nay with 3 not voting, and Alaska Representative Nick Begich voted yea, per the House Clerk's roll call 278. Federal News Network reported that the House Armed Services chairman's mark carries an amendment from Rep. Cory Mills of Florida that bars the Defense Department from leasing its land to private companies to build data centers unless they agree not to install or operate data facility equipment containing components manufactured in China, Russia, Iran or North Korea. Army officials warned the standard would drive world class commercial partners and more than 1.3 billion dollars in private capital away from Army land. If it survives conference it narrows who can bid on the Alaska parcels. The Senate has not passed its version. The underlying offer is unchanged, about 4,700 acres across twelve parcels at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson, Eielson Air Force Base and Clear Space Force Station under the enhanced use lease model, which the Air Force says returns at least fair market value in cash.

Rep. Rashida Tlaib introduced the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act on July 23 with five cosponsors. It would permanently ban large AI data centers and associated infrastructure on land owned or managed by the United States, including military bases, and would require existing qualifying facilities to be removed and their sites remediated. The 4,700 acres offered here sit on exactly that kind of land. No award has been announced for the Alaska proposals, which were due June 29. Separately, the Air Force posted a second Eielson land solicitation on July 23 with an August 10 deadline, but that one is for mixed use development and is not part of this offering.

Still no selection announced. Lease proposals closed June 29, 2026 after an extension from May 29, and five weeks later there is no public award, shortlist or cancellation. Conferees unveiled a draft compromise on July 2 and set a floor vote for July 16, with the second special session ending July 19. Glenfarne owns 75 percent of the project. The sticking point is an S corporation corporate income tax provision that Governor Dunleavy has vowed to veto, and it is unclear the provision has the House votes. The draft also bars the developer from billing the state if the project is abandoned and requires return of shares and assets within six months.

A final investment decision still waits on both the tax law and RCA review of the Enstar gas supply agreement.

The third special session convened Monday, July 27, 2026 with four legislators attending the pro forma opening and no bill from the governor, who said he would work toward a bill acceptable to both the Legislature and Glenfarne. The session is scheduled to end August 25, 2026. Re-verified today against the Anchorage Daily News, July 27, 2026.

Re-checked. Checked and unchanged. The third special session convened July 27th with no bill from the governor and is scheduled to run to August 25th. The compromise bill died July 16th on a 19 to 19 House vote after passing the Senate 11 to 8.

Re-verified against Alaska's News Source, August 6, 2026. The governor urged lawmakers at a Thursday morning meeting to pass an Alaska LNG bill that does not yet exist, and his spokesperson Jeff Turner said it is still being drafted. Senate President Gary Stevens said he postponed Monday's Senate session awaiting the governor's proposed bill and that he had not seen it. House Speaker Bryce Edgmon and Senate Majority Leader Cathy Giessel also reported receiving no bill. The August 10 date tracked here assumed a bill passing the House first, which has not happened.

Checked and unchanged. The third special session is still running and no bill has been introduced. Alaska's News Source reported August 6, 2026 that the governor's spokesperson Jeff Turner said the legislation is still being drafted, and that Senate President Gary Stevens said he had not seen it and held a technical session in place of a Monday floor session at the governor's request. House Speaker Bryce Edgmon and Senate Majority Leader Cathy Giessel also said they had seen no bill. Nothing newer has been published.

The bill collapsed. On August 12th the House Bipartisan Majority Caucus said HB 4001 does not appear to have the support needed to pass the Alaska House, with opposition from both majority and minority members, and the Senate Bipartisan Majority Caucus said it does not plan to reconvene. Governor Dunleavy had asked lawmakers to return to Juneau on August 20th. Senate Majority Leader Cathy Giessel said getting 11 senators and 21 representatives to Juneau right now would be a challenge. A joint Senate and House Resources Committee meeting on Cook Inlet energy is planned for August 20th in Anchorage instead.

The governor signalled the session is over. On the evening of August 13th Governor Dunleavy said that since legislative leadership had chosen not to attend the special session, there is little reason to keep the session going. He had introduced HB 4001 on August 12th, 17 days into a 30 day session, and the House Bipartisan Majority Caucus said the same day that it lacks the votes. Neither chamber expects to meet on the bill. The 35th Legislature convenes in January 2027.

Checked. Nothing has moved. The governor said on August 13th that there is little reason to keep the third special session going, no bill has passed either body, and no fourth session has been called. Senate Minority Leader Mike Cronk told Alaska's News Source that handing the project to the next administration is the real expectation. Glenfarne had pointed to December 2026 for the start of construction.

history.note: Tracked after a reader asked for the carbon capture approval process. The authority comes from two acts of the legislature, chapter 2 of the 2023 session laws directing the commission to seek this authority and chapter 23 of the 2024 session laws establishing the state carbon storage program. The commission held a public meeting on adopting its regulations on March 3rd, 2026 and a hearing on the application itself on May 14th, 2026, with comment closing at the end of that hearing. The commission has said it aims to complete the process in about two years, which other states' experience suggests is optimistic. This matters to the AI build out because the coal plant proposed in the Susitna watershed, tracked separately here, plans to inject its carbon dioxide into a depleted Cook Inlet gas reservoir, and these are the permits that would govern it.

Re-checked against the trade record. The commission held its May 14th hearing on its intention to seek Class VI primary enforcement authority for carbon dioxide storage wells, and no grant or denial by the Environmental Protection Agency has been reported since.

items.summary: The Kenai Peninsula Borough School District is writing the rules for artificial intelligence in its 39 schools while the school year starts. Its Policy Review Committee took up AR 5131.9 Academic Honesty, a new administrative regulation the district says was brought forward in relation to the inclusion of AI, on August 3, 2026, with two competing drafts posted, one from Administration and one from board member Mica VanBuskirk. That same evening the full board took first readings on three more documents the district describes as revised for AI-related policy shifts, AR 5125 Student Records, BP 1114 Communication Using Electronic Media and BP 5131.9 Academic Honesty, plus AR 6161.4 Acceptable Use. Nothing in the package is adopted. The district told KBBI in July that it has spent 8,300 dollars to date on a three year MagicSchool subscription for students and staff, so the classroom AI tool was bought before the rulebook was finished. Upstream sits Alaska's Strategic Framework, Artificial Intelligence for K-12, issued by the Department of Education and Early Development, which means what Kenai adopts previews what other Alaska districts face.

gas_watch.description: A daily numeric record of Southcentral Alaska's natural gas position. Measured storage inventory and deliverability from the CINGSA public dashboard, modeled regional demand from Anchorage degree days, and the derived non CINGSA supply that falls out of the mass balance. It publishes no safety verdict of any kind.

_spec.honesty_note: This model is fitted by least squares to observed EIA Alaska deliveries to residential, commercial and electric power consumers, and refitted whenever another month is published. The published design day and average day are external reference points, not fit targets, so a gap against them is expected and is published rather than tuned away. Nothing derived from this model may be published as a safety verdict, a shortfall prediction, or an all clear.
_spec.no_typed_numbers_rule: Every figure in backtests below is reproduced by code from the committed HDD record. Nothing here is an estimate, a recollection, or a figure copied from prose.
_spec.not_public_note: not_public lists what no source reports DAILY for this region. not_public_monthly_source names the ones that do have a monthly statewide figure, and the page counts them rather than stating a number in prose, so moving an item between these two changes the sentence automatically.
_spec.purpose: Demand model for Cook Inlet Gas Watch. The coefficients live here as data rather than as constants inside scripts/gaswatch_collect.py, so a refit is a data change with its own commit and never a code change. Every collected record carries a copy of this block, so a record always states the model that produced its numbers.
_spec.refit_procedure: scripts/gaswatch_fit.py refits on the monthly EIA workflow. It bumps the version, rewrites the coefficients, recomputes every backtest expectation and appends a model_history entry naming the month count and the error before and after. A fit is rejected unless it has enough months behind it, lands inside physically sane bounds and beats the model it would replace by more than rounding, and a rejected fit leaves the model alone and prints why. To move the coefficients by hand instead, edit them, run python3 scripts/gaswatch_collect.py --self-test, paste the recomputed figures into the backtests below and append the history entry yourself. Either way that self-test recomputes every backtest from config/gaswatch_hdd_history.json and fails if a recorded expectation disagrees, so a typed number that nothing produced cannot survive a commit. Backtest notes carry no numerals, because a refit cannot recompute prose.

backtests.description: The model evaluated at the temperature behind the published design day, for comparison against that planning figure.
backtests.gap_note: Reported, not enforced. A gap beyond sanity_gap_pct means the fit is broken, not that the anchor moved.

backtests.description: The coldest day in the committed Anchorage record, and what the model asks of the system on that day. Recomputed from the HDD history, never typed.
backtests.note: A fact about the weather record, not a claim about whether the system coped, and it must never be published as one. The count of days at or above the published design day is recomputed from the coefficients, so it moves when the model is refitted.

backtests.description: The 2025 to 2026 gas year integrated day by day from the committed record. Season bounds are July 1st through June 30th.
backtests.gap_note: Reported, not enforced. A gap beyond sanity_gap_pct means the fit is broken, not that the anchor moved.
backtests.note: The gap against stated regional consumption across a full gas year is published rather than hidden. The published figure is a planning total and this one is modeled consumption, so they are close relatives and not the same measurement.

backtests.description: Mean modeled demand across every day in the committed record, against the published average day figure.
backtests.gap_note: Reported, not enforced. A gap beyond sanity_gap_pct means the fit is broken, not that the anchor moved.
backtests.note: The gap against the published average day is published rather than tuned away. A planning average carries margin that a fit to observed deliveries does not, so the model is expected to sit under it.

calibration_anchors.role: External reference points, not fit targets. The model is fitted to observed EIA deliveries, so a gap against these published planning figures is expected and is published rather than tuned away. Only an implausible gap is a fault.

fit.geography: EIA reports Alaska statewide. Residential and commercial gas is overwhelmingly Enstar in Southcentral and gas fired power is overwhelmingly Railbelt, so statewide heating and power deliveries stand in for the region. fit.method: least squares, consumption = base * days + slope * HDD65
